## Festivals and alarms: the other languages that are also being lost

In Almuñécar, the festive pealing allowed for no half measures. Bell ringers who still remember the festivals of San Miguel and the Virgen de la Antigua describe a fast, almost euphoric rhythm that overflowed from the bell tower like an invitation hard to refuse. It was not a mere announcement that the party had begun: it was the party itself, transformed into vibration and air. The bells rang out with a contagious joy that spilled through the narrow streets of the old town and climbed the slopes to the most remote farmhouses.

That festive language had its own rules, passed down by ear and from hand to hand across generations of bell ringers. The festive peal was distinguished by its lively cadence, by the way the bells seemed to chase one another without ever catching up. The neighbors did not need to lean out over their balconies to know that the procession was about to set out or that the fireworks would begin shortly. The sound said it all, with a precision that is hard to imagine today in a world saturated with digital notifications and alarms.

In stark contrast to that sonic euphoria, the alarm toll represented the opposite extreme of the emotional spectrum. Bell ringers describe it as a repetitive and intense pealing, devoid of any festive nuance, that lodged itself in the chest of whoever heard it. It served to warn of fires, sudden flash floods, or any emergency requiring the immediate mobilization of the neighborhood. In an era without sirens or public address systems, that sound was the difference between life and death for many families in the municipality.

The intensity of the alarm toll was neither uniform nor arbitrary. Veteran bell ringers recall that the volume and force with which the bell was struck allowed the neighbors to deduce the proximity of the danger. A powerful peal that made the beams of the bell tower vibrate indicated that the emergency was close, perhaps right in the town center or its immediate surroundings. A more restrained sound, on the other hand, suggested that the problem was located on the outskirts, in the farmlands or the higher areas of the municipality.

That acoustic gradation turned the alarm toll into a rudimentary yet effective geographic information system. Those listening from their homes could gauge by ear whether they needed to rush out with buckets of water or if they still had time to organize themselves before heading to the scene of the disaster. The bell ringers needed to explain nothing: the bronze spoke for them, with an eloquence that has now been almost entirely lost. Automation has replaced that nuanced language with a uniform sound, identical for all emergencies and all distances.

The contrast between the festive peal and the alarm toll reveals the communicative richness of a system that today seems condemned to silence. These were not two variations of the same sound, but two distinct languages, each with its own grammar, tempo, and emotional weight. The first invited the community to gather, to celebrate, to forget for a few hours the weariness of daily labor. The second summoned them to immediate action, to urgent solidarity in the face of a shared danger. Both fulfilled a social function that no modern loudspeaker has managed to replicate with the same efficacy.

The bell ringers of Almuñécar insist that the alarm toll was so distinctive that the neighbors never confused it with any other. Even if it rang at midnight, in the midst of a storm, or in the middle of a workday, everyone knew how to recognize it instantly. That communicative clarity was based on the constant repetition of a rhythmic pattern learned since childhood, just as one learns the timbre of a family member's voice. The bells were part of the everyday soundscape, and their current absence has left a void that few know how to name.

The loss of these languages affects not only the memory of the elders. It also affects the community's ability to understand itself as a collective body, with its own codes and its own forms of communication. The festive peal and the alarm toll were, at their core, expressions of the same truth: that Almuñécar functioned as a living organism, capable of rejoicing and alerting in unison. Automation has fragmented that shared experience, replacing it with pre-recorded sounds that make no distinction between joy and danger.

The three bell ringers who still climb the bell tower of Almuñécar keep the memory of those rhythms alive in their hands. They know how the bells were pealed for San Miguel, how they were tolled for the Virgen de la Antigua, and how the bronze was struck when fire threatened the fields. But their knowledge will die with them, because there are no apprentices willing to dedicate hours to mastering a craft that is no longer considered necessary. The last manual peal for a festival or an alarm could sound at any moment, without anyone recognizing it for what it is: the end of an entire language.
